vc-cmv.name: AC/VC
vc-cmv.blurb: Every breath is mandatory. You set tidal volume and inspiratory flow; the ventilator controls flow, so airway pressure is what varies. Look at the pressure scalar for the load and for patient effort.

vc-cmvd.name: AC/VC + flow adaptation
vc-cmvd.examples: Dual-targeted volume control (names vary by ventilator)
vc-cmvd.blurb: Dual targeting: the breath starts as volume control, but if the patient pulls harder than the set flow can satisfy, the ventilator switches to pressure control within the breath and lets flow (and volume) rise to meet demand. If the ventilator also lets that breath flow-cycle, the 2022 taxonomy calls it VC-IMV(4)d,d.

pc-cmv.name: AC/PC
pc-cmv.blurb: Every breath is mandatory and time-cycled. You set the inspiratory pressure and inspiratory time; tidal volume depends on resistance, compliance and patient effort. Look at the flow scalar.

pc-cmva.name: PRVC
pc-cmva.blurb: Looks like volume control on the settings screen, but every breath is pressure control. Between breaths the ventilator adjusts the inspiratory pressure (up to 3 cmH₂O per breath) to hit the target tidal volume. When the patient pulls harder, the ventilator gives less pressure.

vc-imv.name: SIMV-VC + PS
vc-imv.long: Synchronized IMV, volume control, with pressure support
vc-imv.blurb: A set number of volume-control breaths per minute are always delivered (synchronized to effort when possible). Extra patient efforts between them get pressure-supported spontaneous breaths.

pc-imv.name: SIMV-PC + PS
pc-imv.long: Synchronized IMV, pressure control, with pressure support
pc-imv.blurb: A set rate of time-cycled pressure-control breaths, with pressure-supported spontaneous breaths in between.

aprv.name: APRV / BiLevel
aprv.blurb: Two pressure levels, switched on a timer. Releases from P-high to P-low are the mandatory breaths; the patient can breathe spontaneously at either level because the valves stay open.

asv.name: ASV
asv.blurb: Optimal targeting: you set a % of predicted minute ventilation. The ventilator measures the expiratory time constant and uses the Otis equation to choose the rate and tidal volume with the least work, then adjusts pressure to deliver them. Spontaneous breaths reduce the mandatory rate. (Simplified teaching model.)

psv.name: PSV
psv.blurb: Every breath is patient-triggered and flow-cycled. You set the support pressure and the expiratory trigger (cycle) as a % of peak flow. No set rate: if the patient stops breathing, only the apnea backup saves them.

cpap.name: CPAP
cpap.blurb: Pressure support of zero. The ventilator just holds PEEP; the patient does all of the inspiratory work.

vs.name: Volume Support
vs.blurb: Pressure support whose level is adjusted breath to breath to reach a target tidal volume. The harder the patient pulls, the less support it gives.

varps.name: Variable PS
varps.blurb: Bio-variable targeting: the support pressure changes randomly from breath to breath around the set level, mimicking natural breath-to-breath variability.

pav.name: PAV+
pav.blurb: Servo targeting: the ventilator measures R and E and, moment to moment, supplies a set percentage of the pressure needed to overcome them. Pull harder and it pushes harder. With no effort, it gives nothing.

nava.name: NAVA
nava.blurb: Servo targeting from the diaphragm electrical signal (Edi). Pressure is proportional to Edi, the breath is neurally triggered and cycles when Edi falls to 70% of its peak, so timing follows the patient’s own brain. Because of its pressure-control backup, some mode tables list NAVA as PC-IMV(2)s,rs.

off.name: Spontaneous
off.blurb: No ventilator. Respiratory muscles lower pleural pressure, alveolar pressure dips just below atmospheric, and air flows in. Hold the BREATHE button to make a breath.

normal.label: Normal lungs
normal.note: R ≈ 10, Crs ≈ 0.05 L/cmH₂O, τ ≈ 0.5 s (intubated, normal lungs).

ards.label: ARDS
ards.note: Stiff, small lungs: increased elastic load, short time constant.

copd.label: COPD
copd.note: Increased resistive load with a long expiratory time constant: watch expiratory flow.

asthma.label: Status asthmaticus
asthma.note: Severe bronchospasm: very high resistive load in both directions.

fibrosis.label: Pulmonary fibrosis
fibrosis.note: Elastic load from the lung itself; Pplat is high and expiratory flow returns to zero quickly.

obesity.label: Obesity
obesity.note: Heavy chest wall raises pleural pressure: Pplat overestimates the stress on the lung. Turn on the esophageal balloon.

plug.label: Kinked tube / mucus plug
plug.note: Partial blockage in the straw: peak pressure jumps, plateau stays normal.

lessons.session: Session 1 · Indications, basic modes and scalars
lessons.objective: Understand the purpose and indications of MV
lessons.q: Why do some patients require mechanical ventilation, and what are the indications?
lessons.a:
MV is used when a patient cannot maintain adequate oxygenation, ventilation, or work of breathing despite noninvasive support, or when airway protection is needed. It supports gas exchange and reduces respiratory muscle load while the underlying process is treated.

Common indications: refractory hypoxemia, hypercapnic respiratory failure, excessive work of breathing/fatigue, or airway protection.

The ventilator is not only a supportive therapy, it is also a tool that gives you information. Everything in this lab is read from three scalars over time: pressure, flow and volume.

tasks.text: Find the three scalars on the screen: pressure (yellow), flow (teal) and volume (green). Freeze the screen with Freeze (or F) to look closely.
Hover over (or tap, when frozen) a point on the scalars to read its exact values.

lessons.session: Session 1 · Indications, basic modes and scalars
lessons.objective: Outline AC/PC, AC/VC and modifiable parameters
lessons.q: What is the difference between AC/PC and AC/VC?
lessons.a:
Both are assist-control modes in which you set the RR, FiO₂ and PEEP. In assist-control the ventilator delivers a full preset breath whether it is triggered by the patient or by the backup rate.

In AC/VC, tidal volume is set and pressure varies. In AC/PC, inspiratory pressure is set and tidal volume varies.

You can often name the mode from the scalars alone: AC/VC has a square (or decelerating ramp) flow with a rising pressure; AC/PC has a square pressure with an exponentially decaying flow. In this curriculum we stick to square and decelerating-ramp flow in AC/VC.

tasks.text: Open MODE and start AC/PC. Notice which scalar becomes square.
Go back to AC/VC and switch the Flow pattern tile to Decel ramp.

lessons.session: Session 1 · Indications, basic modes and scalars
lessons.objective: Outline AC/PC, AC/VC and modifiable parameters
lessons.q: What “mode” do we breathe in when we breathe spontaneously?
lessons.a:
We breathe with negative pressure generated by our respiratory muscles. The ventilator provides breaths with positive pressure.

If we had to match a ventilator mode to spontaneous breathing, pressure-targeted modes are more similar than volume-targeted modes.

tasks.text: Hold Breathe IN (or the space bar). Watch pleural pressure (Pes) go negative while airway pressure stays at zero.

test._expression: function (e, sim) { return e.type === 'tick' && sim.lastSample && sim.lastSample.Pmus > 4; }

tasks.text: Keep holding for more than 3 seconds. Your muscles can’t contract forever: the breath ends on its own.

lessons.session: Session 1 · Indications, basic modes and scalars
lessons.objective: Outline AC/PC, AC/VC and modifiable parameters
lessons.q: Which mode is more comfortable for the patient?
lessons.a:
Comfort depends on many factors. In general, AC/PC often “feels” smoother because its exponentially decaying flow closely mirrors the flow of our own negative-pressure breaths.

A well-set AC/VC can be equally comfortable. Here the patient is pulling hard and the set flow is low: watch the pressure scalar scoop down during inspiration.

tasks.text: Raise Peak flow to 60 L/min or more and watch the scooped pressure fill back in.
Now switch to AC/PC and compare how flow follows the patient’s pull.

lessons.session: Session 1 · Indications, basic modes and scalars
lessons.objective: Outline AC/PC, AC/VC and modifiable parameters
lessons.q: What are the changeable parameters in each mode?
lessons.a:
Both AC/VC and AC/PC: RR, PEEP and FiO₂.

AC/VC: VT, flow rate and flow pattern.

AC/PC: inspiratory pressure and inspiratory time.

Look at the tiles under the screen: they change with the mode.

tasks.text: In AC/VC, change the VT.

test._expression: function (e, sim) { return e.type === 'set' && e.key === 'VT' && sim.v.mode === 'vc-cmv'; }

tasks.text: Switch to AC/PC and change Pinsp or Ti. Watch VT follow.

test._expression: function (e, sim) { return e.type === 'set' && (e.key === 'Pinsp' || e.key === 'Ti') && sim.v.mode === 'pc-cmv'; }

lessons.session: Session 1 · Indications, basic modes and scalars
lessons.objective: Outline AC/PC, AC/VC and modifiable parameters
lessons.q: Which parameters affect oxygenation and which affect ventilation?
lessons.a:
PEEP and FiO₂ affect oxygenation. PEEP works by raising mean airway pressure, the average airway pressure across the breath cycle.

RR and VT (or inspiratory pressure) affect ventilation, because CO₂ clearance follows minute ventilation (VT × RR).

The ABG panel in the monitor estimates the steady-state gas you would get with the current settings.

tasks.text: Increase the RR and watch the estimated PaCO₂ fall.

test._expression: function (e, sim) { return e.type === 'set' && e.key === 'RR' && sim.v.RR >= 20; }

tasks.text: Increase PEEP to 12 or more and watch Pmean and PaO₂ rise.

lessons.session: Session 1 · Indications, basic modes and scalars
lessons.objective: Outline AC/PC, AC/VC and modifiable parameters
lessons.q: What is lung-protective ventilation, and what are the goal modifiable parameters?
lessons.a:
A collective set of strategies to reduce injury to the lung. The key takeaway at this point: VT should be ≤ 6 mL/kg predicted body weight (PBW), not actual weight. There are also goal pressures to maintain, covered in Session 2.

The VT tile shows mL/kg PBW under the value. PBW comes from sex and height (side panel).

tasks.text: Set VT to 6 mL/kg PBW or less.
Press the button to make the patient a 5′2″ woman and see how the same VT becomes too big.

run._expression: function (VL, sim) { sim.p.sex = 'F'; sim.p.height = 157; VL.setVal('VT', sim.v.VT * 1000, true); VL.toast('Female, 157 cm: PBW ' + sim.pbw().toFixed(1) + ' kg. 6 mL/kg = ' + Math.round(sim.pbw() * 6) + ' mL.'); VL.fire('patient', { id: 'ht' }); }

lessons.session: Session 1 · Indications, basic modes and scalars
lessons.objective: Outline AC/PC, AC/VC and modifiable parameters
lessons.q: Which portions of the breath are trigger, inspiration, cycle and expiration?
lessons.a:
Trigger: initiates inspiration (the patient, or time based on the RR).

Inspiration: flow into the lungs.

Cycle: initiates expiration.

Expiration: flow out of the lungs. Like a pulled spring that is let go, the lungs recoil inward passively.

The phase bands shade inspiration teal. Grey triangles mark time-triggered breaths.

tasks.text: Freeze the screen and hover over a breath. Find the moment the flow crosses zero going down: that is the cycle.
Make inspiration longer (raise Ti) and watch expiration get shorter.

test._expression: function (e, sim) { return e.type === 'set' && e.key === 'Ti' && sim.v.Ti >= 1.3; }

lessons.session: Session 1 · Indications, basic modes and scalars
lessons.objective: Detect patient efforts
lessons.q: How can you distinguish patient-triggered from time-triggered breaths?
lessons.a:
The ventilator marks patient efforts that result in a breath. The mark varies from ventilator to ventilator. Here, patient-triggered breaths get an orange triangle and time-triggered breaths a grey one.

Look also for the small dip in pressure (or rise in flow) just before the breath: that is the patient’s effort reaching the trigger threshold.

tasks.text: Hold Breathe IN during expiration to trigger a breath yourself. Look for the orange mark.
Switch the trigger tile to Pressure and set it to 5 cmH₂O, then trigger again. It takes a much bigger pull.

test._expression: function (e, sim) { return e.type === 'breath' && e.trig === 'patient' && e.manual && sim.v.trig === 'pressure' && sim.v.trigP >= 5; }

lessons.session: Session 1 · Indications, basic modes and scalars
lessons.objective: Review PSV and SBT
lessons.q: What is pressure support mode, and how does it differ from assist-control?
lessons.a:
PSV is a patient-triggered, pressure-supported mode in which you set the inspiratory pressure, PEEP and FiO₂. The RR is solely the patient’s.

Each breath ends when inspiratory flow falls to a set fraction of its peak (the cycle threshold), so the patient also controls inspiratory time.

tasks.text: Lower PS and watch VT fall while the rate stays the patient’s.

test._expression: function (e, sim) { return e.type === 'set' && e.key === 'PS' && sim.v.PS <= 6; }

tasks.text: Raise PS to 15 or more and watch VT climb.

test._expression: function (e, sim) { return e.type === 'set' && e.key === 'PS' && sim.v.PS >= 15; }

lessons.session: Session 1 · Indications, basic modes and scalars
lessons.objective: Review PSV and SBT
lessons.short: When PSV? What is an SBT?
lessons.q: In which scenarios is pressure support appropriate, and what is an SBT?
lessons.a:
PSV fits SBTs, weaning, stable patients with a reliable respiratory drive, or patients intubated solely to protect the upper airway.

An SBT (spontaneous breathing trial) is a time-limited test of extubation readiness: support is reduced to minimal levels (typically PS 5, PEEP 5, FiO₂ 30%) to see whether the patient can sustain ventilation and oxygenation without excessive work of breathing or hemodynamic instability.

tasks.text: Set up an SBT: PS 5, PEEP 5, FiO₂ 30%.

test._expression: function (e, sim) { return sim.v.mode === 'psv' && sim.v.PS === 5 && sim.v.PEEP === 5 && Math.abs(sim.v.FiO2 - 0.3) < 0.005; }

lessons.session: Session 1 · Indications, basic modes and scalars
lessons.objective: Review PSV and SBT
lessons.q: Can you describe the utility of the RSBI?
lessons.a:
The Rapid Shallow Breathing Index = RR ÷ VT (in liters). It is a bedside screening tool during weaning/SBTs. A lower RSBI reflects more efficient breathing. RSBI < 105 generally suggests a higher likelihood of successful extubation, but interpret it alongside the clinical status and trajectory.

RSBI appears in the Timing panel in spontaneous modes.

tasks.text: Press Tire the patient and watch RSBI climb past 105 as the breathing gets rapid and shallow.

run._expression: function (VL, sim) { sim.p.drive.rate = 34; sim.p.drive.amp = 3.2; sim.p.drive.ti = 0.6; VL.toast('Rapid, shallow breathing. Give the rate a few breaths to update.'); }

lessons.session: Session 1 · Indications, basic modes and scalars
lessons.objective: Review PSV and SBT
lessons.q: What would happen if a patient on PSV became apneic?
lessons.a:
If there is no backup mode, ventilation stops. Most ventilators activate apnea/backup ventilation and switch to an assist-control mode after a set apnea time.

Here the apnea time is on the settings tiles. Backup ventilation hands control back once the patient triggers again.

tasks.text: Sedate the patient: press the button (or switch off spontaneous breathing) and wait for the APNEA alarm and backup ventilation.

buttons.label: Give a big dose of sedation

run._expression: function (VL, sim) { sim.p.drive.on = false; VL.toast('Spontaneous effort stopped. Count the seconds…'); }

lessons.session: Session 2 · Single-compartment model, loads and safety
lessons.objective: Describe the single-compartment model of the lung
lessons.short: How does spontaneous effort move air?
lessons.q: How does spontaneous inspiratory effort drive air into the alveoli?
lessons.a:
The patient generates negative pleural pressure, which lowers alveolar pressure “below” airway pressure, and air flows into the lungs. Because the alveolar space is connected to atmosphere, flow occurs so rapidly that alveolar pressure stays near atmospheric.

Watch the digital lung: Ppl (pleural, measured by the balloon as Pes) swings well negative while Palv barely dips.

tasks.text: Take a breath with Breathe IN. Compare how far Ppl and Palv fall on the digital lung.

test._expression: function (e, sim) { return e.type === 'tick' && sim.lastSample && sim.lastSample.Ppl < -4; }

lessons.session: Session 2 · Single-compartment model, loads and safety
lessons.objective: Describe the single-compartment model of the lung
lessons.q: How does a ventilator-supported positive-pressure breath drive air into the alveoli?
lessons.a: The ventilator raises airway pressure above alveolar pressure, so air flows into the lungs. Under normal conditions pleural pressure rises during inspiration: the opposite of a spontaneous breath.

tasks.text: Watch Pes rise with each ventilator breath, then take a breath yourself between them and watch it fall instead.

lessons.session: Session 2 · Single-compartment model, loads and safety
lessons.objective: Describe the single-compartment model of the lung
lessons.q: Can you describe PEEP?
lessons.a: PEEP is the baseline positive pressure maintained at end-expiration to prevent alveolar collapse and improve oxygenation. It may increase mean airway pressure and can reduce venous return if it is too high.

tasks.text: Raise PEEP to 14. Watch the balloon stay bigger at end-expiration and the estimated PaO₂ climb.
Push PEEP to 22 and watch MAP fall: less venous return.

lessons.session: Session 2 · Single-compartment model, loads and safety
lessons.objective: Classify airway, alveolar and pleural pressure
lessons.q: What are peak and plateau pressures? How are they measured and what do they represent?
lessons.a:
Think of a straw (airway) and a balloon (alveoli). Resistance to flow in a straw rises with its length and gas viscosity, and falls with the fourth power of its radius (Poiseuille).

Peak pressure combines the elastic load of the balloon and the resistive load of the straw. To measure only the balloon, remove resistance by stopping flow: an end-inspiratory pause. The pressure during that pause is the plateau pressure, reflecting alveolar/balloon pressure. In ARDS we aim for Pplat < 30 cmH₂O.

tasks.text: Press Insp hold. Read Ppeak and Pplat; the drop between them is the straw.
Raise Peak flow to 90 and hold again: the peak rises, the plateau doesn’t.

lessons.session: Session 2 · Single-compartment model, loads and safety
lessons.objective: Classify airway, alveolar and pleural pressure
lessons.q: How do airway, alveolar and pleural pressures differ in the single-compartment model?
lessons.a:
Airway pressure is measured at the airway opening. Alveolar pressure is the pressure within the alveoli (approximated by Pplat). Pleural pressure surrounds the lung and can be estimated with esophageal manometry.

Transpulmonary pressure (PL) = alveolar − pleural: the distending pressure across the lung itself.

tasks.text: Do an Insp hold and read PL end-insp in the balloon panel (Pplat − Pes).
Do an Exp hold and read PL end-exp.

lessons.session: Session 2 · Single-compartment model, loads and safety
lessons.objective: Classify airway, alveolar and pleural pressure
lessons.q: When is plateau pressure an unreliable surrogate for transpulmonary pressure?
lessons.a:
Pplat reflects the whole respiratory system: lung plus pleural cavity, chest wall and abdomen. It is unreliable whenever pleural pressure is abnormal: active expiration, obesity, or a large pleural effusion. Elevated pleural pressure raises the measured Pplat without raising the distending pressure across the lung.

Two patients with the same Pplat but different pleural pressures can have very different alveolar stress. Esophageal manometry estimates pleural pressure and gives a better transpulmonary pressure.

tasks.text: Do an Insp hold. Pplat looks worrying, but check PL end-insp.
Do an Exp hold: PL end-exp is negative (the lung is being squeezed shut). Raise PEEP until PL end-exp is about 0 or higher, then hold again.

lessons.session: Session 2 · Single-compartment model, loads and safety
lessons.objective: Distinguish the two components of ventilator load
lessons.q: What if the balloon at the end of the straw is very stiff and difficult to inflate?
lessons.a:
An increased elastic load (decreased compliance; “elastic load” and “compliance” describe the same concept from opposite sides). Both peak and plateau rise, and the difference between them stays normal (assuming no added resistive load).

Causes: ARDS, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, atelectasis, fibrosis, auto-PEEP, right mainstem intubation, effusion, pneumothorax, obesity, ascites or abdominal compartment syndrome.

tasks.text: Press Insp hold. Is Ppeak − Pplat < 10?

lessons.session: Session 2 · Single-compartment model, loads and safety
lessons.objective: Distinguish the two components of ventilator load
lessons.q: What happens in the event of a partial blockage in the straw?
lessons.a:
An increased resistive load: higher peak pressure, but the plateau may stay similar if compliance is unchanged, so the difference between peak and plateau increases (≥ 10 cmH₂O).

Causes: obstructive airway disease/bronchospasm, kinked or bitten endotracheal tube, high flow rate or tidal volume, mucus plug or blood clot.

tasks.text: Press Insp hold and compare the peak-plateau gap with the stiff balloon.

lessons.session: Session 2 · Single-compartment model, loads and safety
lessons.objective: Interpret peak and plateau pressures
lessons.q: What would the scalars look like in pulmonary fibrosis versus asthma on AC/VC?
lessons.a:
Fibrosis (decreased lung compliance): high plateau with a correspondingly high peak; normal peak-plateau difference. Expiratory flow is fast and returns to baseline quickly.

Asthma (increased airway resistance): high peak with a relatively lower plateau. Expiratory flow is slow and needs more time to return to baseline.

tasks.text: Do an Insp hold on the fibrosis patient.
Load asthma, do an Insp hold, and compare the expiratory flow.

lessons.session: Session 2 · Single-compartment model, loads and safety
lessons.objective: Understand auto-PEEP
lessons.q: What is auto-PEEP, how do you identify it, and how do you quantify it?
lessons.a:
Auto-PEEP comes from incomplete exhalation: progressive air trapping and higher intrathoracic pressure, above the set PEEP. It can impair venous return, reduce cardiac output and raise the risk of barotrauma. As it worsens, peak and plateau both rise.

Identify: expiratory flow does not return to baseline before the next breath.

Quantify: an expiratory hold measures total PEEP; auto-PEEP = total PEEP − set PEEP.

tasks.text: Press Exp hold and read total PEEP and auto-PEEP.
Fix it: change settings until an Exp hold shows auto-PEEP ≤ 2.

lessons.session: Session 2 · Single-compartment model, loads and safety
lessons.objective: Setting inspiratory and expiratory ratios
lessons.q: How do we choose an I:E ratio, and what should it be with a high resistive load (status asthmaticus)?
lessons.a:
It depends. A longer inspiratory time raises mean airway pressure (may help oxygenation) at the cost of expiratory time (risk of dynamic hyperinflation).

With an excessive resistive load, prolong expiration: an I:E of 1:3 or more (1:4, 1:5) is a reasonable start, then adjust until expiratory flow returns to baseline.

Remember: expiration is passive; you lengthen it indirectly by shortening inspiration or lowering the rate.

tasks.text: Reach an I:E of 1:3 or more (watch the I:E value).

test._expression: function (e, sim) { return e.type === 'tick' && sim.meas.Ti > 0 && sim.meas.Te / sim.meas.Ti >= 2.95; }

tasks.text: Get expiratory flow back to baseline: confirm with an Exp hold showing auto-PEEP ≤ 2.

lessons.session: Session 2 · Single-compartment model, loads and safety
lessons.objective: Describe and adjust safety features, including alarms
lessons.q: What safety features are built into the ventilator, and how should alarms be set?
lessons.a:
Pressure limits, disconnect/low-pressure detection, apnea/backup ventilation, low minute-ventilation alarms, FiO₂ alarms and high-RR limits: they prevent barotrauma and flag hypoventilation or disconnection.

Set alarms relative to expected values: high pressure above the typical peak (catches obstruction/coughing), low pressure/disconnect near baseline, a minute ventilation/VT floor for hypoventilation, and an appropriate apnea time. Reassess after changes in mode, sedation or mechanics.

tasks.text: Set Pmax below the current peak pressure and watch the high-pressure alarm cut breaths short.
Disconnect the circuit (button below) and watch the alarm.

lessons.session: Session 3 · Case-based simulation
lessons.objective: Case 1 · COPD exacerbation
lessons.caseText:
A 65-year-old man with a COPD exacerbation is intubated for worsening hypercapnia and altered mental status. AC/VC: VT 450 mL (~6 mL/kg PBW), RR 14, FiO₂ 60%, PEEP 8.
ABG at 30 minutes: pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 65, PaO₂ 65 on FiO₂ 60%.
lessons.q: What is the primary problem, and which setting(s) should you adjust?
lessons.a:
Hypercapnia (low pH, high PaCO₂). Ventilation follows minute ventilation (VT × RR), so increase one of them. VT is already lung-protective, so a safe change is to increase the RR.

Alternatively, with no acute lung injury requiring strict limits, VT can go to 8 mL/kg PBW provided Pplat stays < 30. Beware: a higher RR can cause dynamic hyperinflation in obstructive disease.

tasks.text: Increase minute ventilation (RR or VT) and watch the estimated PaCO₂ improve.

lessons.session: Session 3 · Case-based simulation
lessons.objective: Case 1 · COPD exacerbation
lessons.caseText: A few minutes later the nurse notices the patient needs escalating norepinephrine. Look at the scalars.
lessons.q: Describe what is happening based on the scalars, and how you would fix it.
lessons.a:
Dynamic hyperinflation (auto-PEEP) from insufficient expiratory time with obstructive physiology. Trapped gas raises end-expiratory alveolar and intrathoracic pressure, impairs venous return and causes hypotension. Make sure expiratory flow returns to baseline before each breath.

To lengthen expiratory time:

  • AC/VC and AC/PC: lower the RR (consider sedation, even neuromuscular blockade, for patient-triggered tachypnea); treat the obstruction (bronchodilators).
  • AC/VC: decrease VT (if > 6 mL/kg) and increase inspiratory flow; both shorten inspiration.
  • AC/PC: decrease the set inspiratory time.
  • An I:E of 1:3 or more is a reasonable start; adjust until expiratory flow reaches baseline.

This may worsen the acidosis, but with circulatory collapse looming, it is the least-harm trade.

tasks.text: Confirm it with an Exp hold.
Fix it, then prove it: Exp hold with auto-PEEP ≤ 2 and MAP ≥ 65.

test._expression: function (e, sim) { return e.type === 'holdExp' && e.autoPEEP <= 2 && sim.gas().MAP >= 65; }

lessons.session: Session 3 · Case-based simulation
lessons.objective: Case 2 · ARDS
lessons.caseText: A 50-year-old woman with multifocal pneumonia, severe hypoxemia and hypercapnia is intubated; imaging and ABG are consistent with ARDS. Height 5′10″ (70 in).
lessons.q: Which mode would you use, and what initial settings?
lessons.a:
No mode is inherently superior, but the landmark lung-protective ARDS trials used AC/VC, which guarantees low VT and reliable plateau monitoring. AC/PC can work but holding a stable 6 mL/kg needs close monitoring. The true therapy is lung-protective ventilation.

  • PBW for a 70-inch female ≈ 68.5 kg.
  • VT 6 mL/kg ≈ 410 mL.
  • RR ~18–24, titrated to a safe I:E (typically 1:2).
  • PEEP/FiO₂ from the ARDSNet table, e.g. FiO₂ 80% with PEEP 14. Wean FiO₂ to ≤ 60% as soon as feasible.

tasks.text: Choose AC/VC.
Set VT ≈ 6 mL/kg PBW (400–420 mL), RR 18–24, PEEP 14, FiO₂ 80%.

test._expression: function (e, sim) { var k = pbwVT(sim); return sim.v.mode === 'vc-cmv' && k >= 5.8 && k <= 6.2 && sim.v.RR >= 18 && sim.v.RR <= 24 && sim.v.PEEP === 14 && Math.abs(sim.v.FiO2 - 0.8) < 0.005; }

lessons.session: Session 3 · Case-based simulation
lessons.objective: Case 2 · ARDS
lessons.caseText: An end-inspiratory pause measures a plateau pressure of 34 cmH₂O.
lessons.q: What adjustments would you make?
lessons.a: 34 exceeds the recommended < 30 cmH₂O and increases the risk of ventilator-induced lung injury. Reduce VT (e.g. from 6 to 4–5 mL/kg PBW) to lower the plateau, then reassess Pplat promptly. A VT change will also change PaCO₂, so repeat the ABG.

tasks.text: Confirm the plateau with an Insp hold.
Lower VT (not below 4 mL/kg) and hold again until Pplat < 30.

test._expression: function (e, sim) { return e.type === 'holdInsp' && e.Pplat < 30 && pbwVT(sim) >= 3.95; }

lessons.session: Session 3 · Case-based simulation
lessons.objective: Case 2 · ARDS
lessons.caseText: After VT is finalized, the repeat ABG at 30 minutes shows pH 7.21, PaCO₂ 63, PaO₂ 84 on FiO₂ 80%.
lessons.q: Should you make any changes?
lessons.a:
In ARDS we prioritize low lung volumes and tolerate permissive hypercapnia to keep Pplat < 30. With severe hypercapnic acidemia (pH < 7.20), raise the RR first, reserving VT increases for refractory cases while staying lung-protective.

An excessively high RR can itself be injurious and can cause auto-PEEP. A normal ABG is not always the goal in ARDS.

tasks.text: Raise the RR (not VT) and watch the estimated pH.

test._expression: function (e, sim) { return e.type === 'set' && e.key === 'RR' && sim.v.RR > 22 && sim.v.VT <= 0.33; }

tasks.text: Check that flow still returns to baseline: Exp hold with auto-PEEP ≤ 2.

test._expression: function (e, sim) { return e.type === 'holdExp' && e.autoPEEP <= 2 && sim.v.RR > 22; }

lessons.doneMsg: That’s the whole curriculum. Try the Asynchrony Challenge next.

sub._expression: function () { return fmt(sim.v.VT * 1000 / sim.pbw(), 1) + ' mL/kg PBW'; }
function () { var b = sim.v.pattern === 'ramp' && sim.v.mode !== 'vc-cmvd' ? 2 : 1; return 'Ti ' + fmt(b * sim.v.VT / (sim.v.flow / 60), 2) + ' s'; }
function () { var te = 60 / sim.v.RR - sim.v.Ti; return te > 0 ? 'I:E 1:' + fmt(te / sim.v.Ti, 1) : 'inverse!'; }
function () { var a = sim.asvTarget(); return 'f ' + fmt(a.f, 0) + ' · VT ' + fmt(a.VT * 1000, 0); }
